First, I'll probably implement a compute shader version of this. This isn't so much of an optimization in and of itself, but it does enable the next two optimizations.
In a compute shader, we could rasterize one scan line at a time as opposed to one tile at a time, which is the natural way that a pixel shader does its grouping.
For pixel shaders, it's a pretty good assumption that if you are close by to another pixel in screen space, you will probably access the same memory.
In our case, this is not exactly true. Pixels that are adjacent to each other vertically might access very different memory depending on which scan line they occupy.
If we process pixels as scan lines as opposed to tiles, another thing we could do is load curves into scalar registers as opposed to vector registers.
Vector register pressure hasn't really been an issue for me, but this is something to keep in mind if you run into that problem.
Unrelated, but in the future I may take some time to implement more accurate anisotropic filtering.
Earlier, I mentioned that we could manipulate pixel windows and take linear combinations of coverage estimates in order to approximate the ellipse of anisotropy.
I've only experimented with this a little bit, but I haven't actually needed it for my current project.
I might do this in the future, though. Something else I also haven't implemented but had started was vertical partitioning.

It probably makes sense to split curves up in such a way that they are sorted from left to right or somehow vertically partitioned so that you can quickly discard all the curves that are fully to the right
of the pixel you're looking at. This specific optimization is likely very font-dependent in terms of how effective it is.
In my early experiments, I actually didn't see any speed-up at all, which is why I haven't bothered finalizing it.
It's possible, though, that for some fonts, this type of thing might be even necessary.
And last, another thing I think might be worth exploring is actually some form of curve compression.
Even though I'm storing all the curved data as sixteen-bit floats, there is still quite a bit of redundancy because a lot of the control points are actually shared between neighboring curves.
I'll probably circle back to this in the future when I add support for CJK languages or other languages that have a lot more glyphs than English.
